summary: Provides a reference framework for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) for Service Function Chaining (SFC). It sets out how SFC networks can be tested and monitored. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8924 is a blueprint for the operational tooling of a service function chain. It says which parts of such a network need testing, what kind of test each part needs, and how far the existing tools, from ping to BFD to in-situ OAM, can be stretched to cover them. It defines no new protocol.

questions: how are service function chains monitored
what oam tools work with sfc
how do you test connectivity in a service chain
subtitle: How to test and monitor a network that pushes traffic through a chain of service functions.

tldr.problem: Operations staff have ping, traceroute and liveness tools for ordinary networks, but nothing standard for checking that the individual service functions in a chain are alive and that traffic is really following the intended path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC breaks the service layer into three components, the service function, the chain and the classifier, lists the OAM functions each needs, and works out which existing tools can be adapted to serve them.
tldr.outcome: The result is a reference framework rather than a protocol. The gap analysis finds that no standards-based tool can yet verify a service function or a chain natively, so solution documents are expected to fill the gap and to state which component they target.

facts.value: Connectivity, continuity, trace and performance measurement

today: RFC 8924 is an Informational document from October 2020 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. It is a reference framework rather than a protocol, and the solution documents it anticipates are expected to cite it to say which component they cover.

sections.title: What This Framework Covers
sections.content:
Service Function Chaining (SFC) enables the creation of composite services consisting of an ordered set of Service Functions (SFs) applied to traffic selected as a result of classification. SFC describes a method for deploying SFs that enables dynamic ordering and topological independence of those SFs, as well as the exchange of metadata between participating entities. The foundations are in the SFC Problem Statement and the SFC Architecture, and the reader is assumed to be familiar with the architecture.

This document provides a reference framework for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance of SFC. It provides an SFC layering model; the aspects monitored by SFC OAM; functional requirements for SFC OAM; a gap analysis for SFC OAM; operational aspects of SFC OAM at the service layer; the applicability of various OAM tools; and manageability considerations for service functions and SFC. SFC OAM solution documents are expected to refer to this document to indicate which component they target and what functionality they cover.

OAM controllers are defined as SFC-aware network devices that are capable of generating OAM packets, and they should be within the same administrative domain as the target SFC-enabled domain. The focus of the document is to provide an architectural framework for SFC OAM, particularly the Operations component within OAM. Actual solutions and mechanisms are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A service function chain is a pipeline of processing functions, with traffic classified at the start and then sent through the chain. This RFC asks how an operator checks that pipeline: that each function is alive, that the chain is connected, that the classifier is putting traffic in the right chain, and that the delays and losses are within bounds.

sections.title: The SFC Layering Model
sections.content:
Several layers come into play when implementing SFC, including the service layer and the layers beneath it.

The service layer consists of the SFC data-plane elements: classifiers, Service Functions, Service Function Forwarders, and SFC Proxies. This layer uses the overlay network layer for connectivity between the data-plane elements.

The overlay network layer leverages overlay technologies such as VXLAN to interconnect the data-plane elements and to allow Service Function Paths to be established. It is mostly transparent to the data-plane elements, since not all of them process the overlay header.

The underlay network layer is dictated by the networking technology deployed within the network, for example IP or MPLS.

The link layer is tightly coupled with the physical technology used. Ethernet is one choice, but alternatives may be deployed, such as POS and DWDM, and in a virtual environment virtualized I/O technologies such as SR-IOV are also applicable. The same or distinct link layer technologies may be used in each leg of the path.

In the layering example, the service-layer elements such as the classifier and the service functions are depicted as virtual entities interconnected using an overlay network, and the underlay network may comprise multiple intermediate nodes, not shown, that provide underlay connectivity between the service-layer elements. While the example depicts service functions enabled as virtual entities, the SFC architecture makes no assumptions about how the data-plane elements are deployed: it accommodates physical or virtual deployment, and SFC OAM accounts for this flexibility, being applicable whether the elements are deployed directly on physical hardware, as one or more virtual entities, or any combination.
sections.plainLanguage: Four layers are involved. The service layer holds the chain itself: the classifier, the functions and the forwarders that move traffic between them. Above the physical network sits an overlay that connects those elements, and beneath it the underlay and link layers carry the traffic. The framework works whether the functions run on bare machines or inside virtual machines.

sections.title: The Components That Need Testing
sections.content:
The SFC operates at the service layer, and for the purpose of defining the OAM framework that layer is broken up into three distinct components.

The SF component covers OAM functions that include testing the service functions from any SFC-aware network device, such as classifiers, controllers and other service nodes. Testing a service function may be more expansive than checking connectivity to it, such as checking whether the function is providing its intended service. One requirement is to allow an SFC-aware network device to check the availability of a specific service function instance, located on the same or different network devices. Where several instances of a function are used for load sharing, availability can be checked on any one of them or on a specific instance. The RFC notes the tension here: one might argue that a function is available if the node hosting it is available and functional, while another might argue that availability can only be deduced if the packet is examined after passing through and the expected service is confirmed. The first is unlikely to give enough confidence, because a service node and a service function are different entities. The second gives an extensive verification but comes at a cost, since some functions modify packets directly and some deliberately drop certain packets, so an OAM mechanism has to take those specifics into account. The cost is that the mechanism for some functions has to be modified continuously to keep up with new functionality. A generalized check at a granularity that provides a basic service is possible, but evaluating true availability is a complex activity with no simple unified solution and no standard means of doing it.

The second requirement for the SF component is performance measurement: checking the metrics, such as loss and delay, induced by a specific service function for legitimate traffic. Measurement can be passive, using live traffic, active, using synthetic probe packets, or hybrid. The performance of a function can be quantified by measuring the loss and delay of the traffic from the forwarder to the function, or by leveraging the loss and delay metrics from the function itself; the former does not need the function's involvement, the latter does.

The SFC component covers testing the chains and the service function paths, and validating the correlation between a chain and the actual forwarding path followed by a packet matching that chain, the Rendered Service Path. Some hops of a chain may not be visible when Hierarchical Service Function Chaining is in use, in which case it is the responsibility of the Internal Boundary Node to glue the connectivity between levels for end-to-end OAM functionality. An SFC may comprise varying functions, so the OAM layer must perform validation and verification of the functions within a path, in addition to connectivity verification and fault isolation. OAM functions could be initiated from any SFC-aware device of an SFC-enabled domain, for end-to-end paths or for partial paths terminating on a specific function, with return codes defined for the response to the OAM packet. When ECMP is in use at the service layer for a given chain, there must be the ability to discover and traverse all available paths.

The classifier component covers testing the validity of the classification rules and detecting incoherence among the rules installed when more than one classifier is used. A classifier maintains the rules that map a flow to a chain, so it is vital that it is correctly configured with updated rules and functioning as expected: the SFC OAM must validate the rules by assessing whether a flow is appropriately mapped to the relevant chain and detect any misclassification, and sample OAM packets can be presented to classifiers to assess their behaviour for a given entry. Availability checking of the classifier, and performance measurement of it for each chain, are also required.

Two further layers are named. The underlay network provides connectivity between the SFC components, so its availability and performance directly affect SFC OAM, and any SFC-aware device may perform an availability check or performance measurement of it using the existing OAM functions. The overlay network provides connectivity for the service plane between the components and is mostly transparent to the data-plane elements, and the same applies to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things need separate treatment: the individual functions, the chain as a whole, and the classifier that decides which traffic enters which chain. A function's health is hard to judge, because the node it runs on being up says little about whether the function itself works, while checking the packet after it has passed through means handling functions that deliberately drop packets. The chain needs its actual path compared with the intended one, and the classifier needs its rules checked against real traffic.

sections.title: The OAM Functions Needed
sections.content:
The functions in this section apply to more than one SFC component. Many OAM functions already exist at other layers, and to apply them at the service layer they need to be enhanced to operate on a single service function or forwarder, or on multiple of them spanning one or more chains.

Connectivity functions are mainly an on-demand function to verify that connectivity exists between certain network elements and that the functions are available. Label Switched Path Ping is a common tool for this in an MPLS network. The functions include verifying the path MTU from a source to the destination function or through the chain, which requires the OAM packet to be of variable length; detecting packet reordering and corruption; verifying that a chain or function is applying the expected policy; verifying and validating forwarding paths; and proactively testing alternate or protected paths to ensure the reliability of network configurations.

Continuity functions send OAM messages periodically to validate or verify the reachability of a given function within a chain, or of the entire chain. This allows a monitoring device such as the classifier or the controller to detect failures quickly, such as link failures, network element failures, function outages or chain outages. BFD is one such protocol. The functions include provisioning a continuity check to a given function or for the whole chain, proactively testing alternate or protected paths, and notifying other OAM functions or applications of detected failures so they can take appropriate action.

Trace functions allow the operation to trigger an action, such as response generation, from every transit device on the tested layer, which is useful for gathering information from every transit device or for isolating the failure point to a specific function or to the whole chain. The functions include triggering an action from every transit device at the SFC layer using TTL or other means, triggering every transit device to generate a response with OAM codes, discovering and traversing ECMP paths within a chain, and skipping functions that do not support OAM while tracing.

Performance measurement functions measure packet loss, delay and delay variance, proactively or on demand. The framework should be able to measure packet loss for a chain; on-demand measurement can estimate it statistically, and for accurate estimation the OAM packets need to be treated the same way and share the same fate as regular data traffic. Delay within a chain could be measured from the time a packet takes to traverse it from the ingress node to the egress forwarder, using measurement protocols such as OWAMP and TWAMP. Because chains are unidirectional, one-way delay measurement is important, and to measure it time synchronization must be supported by means such as NTP, GPS or PTP. One-way delay variation could be calculated by sending OAM packets and measuring the jitter for traffic passing through a chain. The functions include measuring the packet processing delay induced by a single function, or the one-way delay to traverse a path bound to a given chain, and measuring the packet loss within a function or a path.

The gap analysis compares the functions above with the tools that exist. Ping and trace perform connectivity checks and trace intermediate hops, and support network types such as IP, MPLS and TRILL. Ethernet OAM and Connectivity Fault Management offer mechanisms such as a continuity check for Ethernet links, and there is an effort around NVO3 OAM for networks using NVO3. BFD is used for the detection of data-plane forwarding failures. The IPPM framework offers tools such as OWAMP and TWAMP to measure performance metrics, and MPLS Packet Loss Measurement and Packet Delay Measurement offer the same for MPLS networks. Set against that, the table shows connectivity and continuity support for the underlay and overlay networks and for the classifier, but nothing at all for the service function or the chain: there are no standards-based tools available at the time of writing that can be used natively, without enhancement, for the verification of service functions and chains, and toolsets and solutions are required to perform the OAM functions at the service layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Four kinds of test are needed: a one-off check that the path works, a repeating check that stays working, a trace that shows which hop broke, and measurements of delay and loss. All of them exist for ordinary networks. The gap the RFC finds is at the service layer, where the tools for the function and the chain are simply absent, and existing tools have to be extended to work on a single function or across a chain.

sections.title: Service-Layer Mechanics and Candidate Tools
sections.content:
SFC OAM messages should be encapsulated with the necessary SFC header and with OAM markings when testing the chain, and may be so encapsulated when testing a single function. The OAM function performed at the service layer or overlay network layer must mark the packet as an OAM packet so that relevant nodes can tell OAM packets from data packets. The base header of the Network Service Header assigns a bit to indicate OAM packets, and when NSH encapsulation is used at the service layer that bit must be set. Any other overlay encapsulation used at the service layer must have a way to mark the packet as OAM.

On receipt of an OAM packet, an SFC-aware function may choose to discard it if it does not support OAM functionality or if local policy prevents it from being processed. When a function does support OAM, it is desirable to process the packet and give an appropriate response so that end-to-end verification is possible, and to limit the performance impact of OAM the functions should rate-limit the number of OAM packets they process. A forwarder may choose not to forward the OAM packet to a function if the function does not support OAM or policy does not allow it, and may instead skip the function, modify the packet's header and forward the packet to the next node in the chain. Skipping a function may have implications for some OAM functions, for instance delay measurement may not be accurate. How a forwarder detects whether the connected function supports or may process OAM packets is outside the scope of the document: it could be a configuration parameter set by the controller, or a dynamic negotiation between the function and the forwarder. If the forwarder receiving the OAM packet bound to a given chain is the last one in the chain, it must send a relevant response to the initiator, which could be a simple response such as an ICMP reply, or could include additional data from the received packet such as statistics consolidated along the path.

Different OAM functions may require different solutions, so while the OAM marker in the overlay header indicates a packet as OAM it is not sufficient to indicate what the packet is for. The Next Protocol field in the NSH header may be used to indicate the intended OAM function or the toolset being used, and any other overlay encapsulation at the service layer must have a similar way to indicate it.

Several existing toolsets could be adapted. ICMP could serve the connectivity functions: the initiator generates an echo request and controls the service-layer encapsulation header to get a response from the relevant node. A classifier could set the TTL field in the NSH header to 63 to get the response from the last forwarder and thereby test the chain's availability, set the TTL to another value to get a response from a specific function for a partial test, or send packets with successively incrementing TTL to trace the path. As currently defined, ICMP may not be able to perform all the required functions, but it can cover some of the connectivity ones. BFD and Seamless BFD could serve the continuity function: an initiator generates a BFD control packet and sets the Your Discriminator value to identify the last forwarder, which replies with the relevant DIAG code, and the TTL in the NSH header could be used for a partial availability check by making it expire at the function under test. In situ OAM could serve function and chain availability and performance measurement, with the O bit in the NSH header set to indicate OAM traffic; the proof-of-transit mechanism can securely verify whether a packet traversed the relevant path. And a proposed SFC traceroute protocol checks path liveliness and traces the service hops in any path, with the Service Index Limit used by an initiator to perform availability tests; the proposal has expired but is implemented in Open Daylight and available.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM packets have to be marked so that the nodes along the path recognize them and do not confuse them with user traffic, and a function that does not want to answer may drop them. The RFC then shows how four existing tools could be stretched to the job: ICMP for on-demand checks, BFD for continuous liveness, in-situ OAM carried inside real data packets, and a traceroute for the service layer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any security considerations defined in the SFC Architecture and in the Network Service Header specification apply. The OAM information from the service layer at different components may collectively or independently reveal sensitive information, such as the type of service functions hosted in the network, the classification rules and associated service chains, and specific service function paths, so careful security considerations are needed.

The mapping and rules information at the classifier may reveal the traffic rules and the traffic mapped to the chain. Information collected at the chain component may reveal the functions associated within each chain, and together with the classifier rules it may be used to manipulate the header of synthetic attack packets to bypass the chain and trigger internal attacks. Information at the function component may be used by a malicious user to trigger a denial-of-service attack by overloading a specific function with rogue OAM traffic.

To address these concerns, SFC and function OAM should provide mechanisms for mitigating misuse of the OAM channel for denial of services, leakage of OAM packets across chain instances, and leakage of chain information beyond the chain's domain. The documents proposing an OAM solution for function components should rate-limit the OAM probes at a frequency guided by the implementation choice, and the rate limiting may be applied at the classifier, the forwarder or the function. The initiator may then not receive a response for rate-limited probes, resulting in false negatives, and the implementation should be aware of this. Documents proposing OAM solutions should also describe how anomalies and attacks are detected and mitigated, and should consider some form of message filtering to control the OAM packets entering the administrative domain or prevent internal service-layer information from leaking outside it.
sections.plainLanguage: Testing a chain means revealing a lot about it: which functions are deployed, which traffic goes where, and how the classifier is configured. That information could help an attacker craft packets that skip the chain, or flood one function with test traffic. The RFC therefore asks for rate limits on probes and for filtering that keeps both the traffic and the information inside the administrative domain.

layers.label: Service layer

layers.detail: Whatever the network runs on, for example IP or MPLS

items.title: SF component
items.text: The individual service functions: their availability, which is hard to judge, and their loss and delay contribution.

items.title: SFC component
items.text: The chain and its paths: connectivity between functions, validation of the rendered service path, and finding the failing hop.

items.title: Classifier component
items.text: The rules that map a flow to a chain: their validity, the absence of misclassification, and the classifier's own performance.

items.title: Underlay network
items.text: Provides the connectivity between the components, so its health affects everything above it.

items.title: Overlay network
items.text: Carries the service plane between the components and is mostly transparent to them.
